summary: Describes the URI resource record, a DNS record type that maps a hostname to one or more URIs. The record type had already been registered, and this document formally describes it, including how multiple entries are prioritized.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone book entry that, instead of a phone number, lists web addresses to use for a name.

questions: what is a uri dns record
subtitle: A DNS record type that maps a service name under a domain straight to one or more full URIs.

tldr.problem: Mapping a domain name to a URL with NAPTR records returns every URI tied to the owner and requires rewrite rules to extract the right one.
tldr.mechanism: The URI resource record puts the service in the owner name, for example _ftp._tcp, and holds a priority, a weight and the target URI directly in its data.
tldr.outcome: A client that knows the domain, protocol and service can query exactly the records it wants. RRTYPE 256 was allocated in February 2011 and this RFC documents it.

today: RFC 7553 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted or updated. It documents the URI resource record whose type number IANA had already allocated.

sections.title: Why a URI Record
sections.content:
Historically, the DNS mapped a domain name to a URL with Naming Authority Pointer (NAPTR) records and the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System. The returned RRset holds all URIs connected with the owner, not just those for one service, and the client must apply rewrite rules.

The URI resource record puts the NAPTR service field into the owner name and stores the target URI directly in the data. It does not replace NAPTR or S-NAPTR. It is a complementary mechanism for when the client already knows which service it wants.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of getting a huge list of addresses and sorting through it, you ask for the one kind you want and get just those.

sections.title: The URI RR Format
sections.content:
The presentation format is Owner name TTL Class URI Priority Weight Target. The type number is 256, the record is class independent, has no special TTL requirements and causes no Additional Section processing.

Priority is in the range 0-65535, and a client MUST try the lowest-numbered priority it can reach. Among equal priorities, Weight (also 0-65535) SHOULD give larger weights a proportionately higher probability of selection. Target is the URI in double quotes, and it MUST NOT be empty. Because it is not a character-string, the 255-character limit does not apply.

On the wire, the data is a 2-octet Priority, a 2-octet Weight, and a variable-length Target of the URI octets without the quotes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry says how important it is, how often to pick it among equals, and then gives the web address itself.

sections.title: Service Names in the Owner Name
sections.content:
Like SRV, the URI record encodes the service in the owner name. Valid parameters come from the IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry or from Enumservice registrations. Enumservice parameters are reversed and each is prefixed with an underscore, which avoids collisions with ordinary DNS labels and allows delegation to different zones.

For service name A and transport B at example.com, the query is _A._B.example.com with type URI. The FTP example publishes _ftp._tcp IN URI 10 1 "ftp://ftp1.example.com/public" in both example.com and example.net.
sections.plainLanguage: You add the name of the service in front of the domain, like writing the department on an envelope, to reach the right entry.

sections.title: Relation to NAPTR and SRV
sections.content:
The URI record is not a replacement for S-NAPTR; the second step of S-NAPTR resolution can resolve a URI record instead of using SRV records. Together with S-NAPTR it can be viewed as a replacement for U-NAPTR. NAPTR records of any kind find which services exist for a domain, one step before the URI record is used.

It can be viewed as a replacement for SRV, since both need the base domain, protocol and service, and both use the same service name registry. Where SRV returns a host name and port number, the URI record returns a full URI, so it is more powerful.

The DNS considerations warn that underscored labels in wildcard names do not synthesize answers and that service labels may be overloaded, so applications should check the application-level protocol is what they expect.
sections.plainLanguage: An older system tells you which services exist. This one, like SRV, gives the exact address once you know the service, and it gives a whole web address, not just a machine and port.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
IANA allocated RRTYPE 256 after an expert review in February 2011 and updated the reference to this RFC. No new registry is needed, since existing service registries are reused.

If the URI record is not signed with DNSSEC and validated, trusting it effectively leads to a downgrade attack. The recommended approach is to secure the record with DNSSEC, ideally validating in the application, and to verify the TLS certificate against the host name in the URI, not the one originally looked up. Userinfo SHOULD NOT be placed in a URI in this record, as DNS data is public.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone could swap a fake address into the phone book unless it is signed. Check the signature and check who you reach.

fields.name: Priority
fields.desc: Unsigned integer; lowest number is tried first.

fields.name: Weight
fields.desc: Relative weight among entries with the same priority.
